label: New Spaces from Old
notes: This chapter, printed pages forty-nine through eighty-four, teaches four ways to build topological spaces: subspace, product, disjoint union, and quotient. The unifying idea is that every construction is recognized by which canonical maps it forces to be continuous, giving a single audit workflow rather than four disconnected definitions.

label: The Four Constructions
notes: Subspaces clip ambient opens through a subset, products test continuity coordinatewise, disjoint unions tag points by their source piece, and quotients see only saturated sets. Reading the four constructions side by side highlights a shared theme: continuity questions reduce to canonical maps, so each construction is a continuity gate, not a list of opens.

label: Subspaces: Openness Is Relative
notes: In the subspace topology a set is open exactly when it equals the intersection of the subset with an ambient open set. Relative openness is genuinely different: the closed interval becomes open inside a disconnected ambient set, and isolated points appear that were not isolated before, so closures and neighborhoods must always name their ambient space.

label: Embeddings: Injective Is Not Enough
notes: A topological embedding is a continuous injection that is a homeomorphism onto its image. The parabola map qualifies because the first projection inverts it continuously. The half-open interval wrapping around the circle is continuous and injective yet fails, because parameters near one map near the image of zero, so the inverse tears nearby image points apart.

label: Characteristic Properties
notes: Each construction carries a characteristic property that recognizes it by mapping behavior. Subspaces and products are initial: maps into them test after composing with inclusion or projections. Disjoint unions and quotients are final: maps out of them test by restricting to summands or composing with the quotient map. These gates organize every continuity proof in the chapter.

label: Products: Coordinates Are Tests
notes: For a finite product, a map in is continuous exactly when every coordinate function is continuous, because basic opens are product rectangles. The product topology is the weakest making all projections continuous, so it adds no test beyond the coordinate tests. This is the familiar componentwise continuity of vector-valued functions, made topological.

label: Infinite Products Need Care
notes: In the product topology a basic open restricts only finitely many coordinates; the box topology restricts all at once. The diagonal map into countably many copies of the line is continuous for the product topology but not the box topology, where the shrinking box around zero has preimage a single point. Componentwise continuity characterizes the product, not the box.

label: Disjoint Unions: Keep the Tags
notes: A disjoint union tags every point by its source component, so a set is open exactly when its slice in each summand is open there. The canonical injections are embeddings, and a map out is continuous iff every restriction to a summand is continuous. Each whole component is open, since its slice fills one summand and empties the rest.

label: Quotients: Only Saturated Sets
notes: A quotient starts from a surjection: a set downstairs is open exactly when its preimage is open upstairs. The only upstairs sets that matter are saturated sets, which contain whole equivalence classes. This single rule builds circles from intervals, tori from squares, projective space from the sphere, and the circle as the real line modulo integer translates.

label: The Torus from the Square
notes: Gluing opposite edges of the unit square with matching arrow directions yields the torus, equally the product of two circles. Reversing one pair of arrows gives the Klein bottle, and identifying just one pair with a flip gives the Mobius band. The arrow pattern on the fundamental polygon encodes which quotient, and therefore which surface, results.

label: Adjunction Spaces and Pathologies
notes: An adjunction space glues a subspace of one space onto another by first forming a disjoint union, then quotienting by the attaching map; it models cones, doubles, and attached cells. Quotients also breed pathologies: the line with two origins is locally Euclidean and second countable yet not Hausdorff, since saturated neighborhoods of the two origins always overlap.

label: Audit Workflow and Takeaways
notes: A topology on a constructed set is best understood through its canonical maps. The standing audit is short but strict: name the canonical map, state the open-set test, apply the characteristic property, then record which properties are inherited and which require proof. For quotients especially, verify saturation and separation before ever calling the result a manifold.
